entity.name: Michael Faraday
entity.description: A bookbinder's apprentice who taught himself science and invented the electric motor. Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction, benzene, and the laws of electrolysis despite knowing no math beyond basic algebra. Einstein kept his portrait on the wall alongside Newton's. He turned down a knighthood, preferring to remain 'plain Mr Faraday.'

story.name: Michael Faraday
story.description: A bookbinder sends a 300-page notebook to a famous chemist and lands a job, discovers electromagnetic induction at the Royal Institution, refuses a knighthood and a presidency, and dies at Hampton Court. The self-taught genius who made electricity practical.

moments.name: Michael Faraday Is Born to a Blacksmith's Family in Southwark
moments.subtitle: The future father of electricity begins life in poverty with almost no schooling
moments.description: On 22 September 1791, Michael Faraday was born in Newington Butts, Surrey (now part of Southwark, London), the third of four children of James Faraday, a blacksmith who had recently moved the family from Westmorland. The family was poor and belonged to the small Sandemanian Christian sect. Faraday received only the most basic education before being apprenticed to a bookbinder at age 14. During his seven-year apprenticeship on Blandford Street, Faraday read voraciously, developing a passion for science, especially electricity. The self-educated boy would become one of the most influential scientists in history.

moments.name: Faraday Sends a 300-Page Notebook to Humphry Davy and Lands a Job
moments.subtitle: A bookbinder's handwritten lecture notes open the door to one of science's greatest careers
moments.description: On 1 March 1813, Michael Faraday was appointed Chemical Assistant at the Royal Institution in London after sending the eminent chemist Humphry Davy a 300-page book of meticulous notes from Davy's own lectures. Faraday, then 21 and just finishing a bookbinding apprenticeship, had attended Davy's lectures thanks to tickets given by a customer. Davy was impressed and hired Faraday when a vacancy arose. Within weeks, both men were injured in a nitrogen trichloride explosion. Faraday would remain at the Royal Institution for 54 years, rising from assistant to the first Fullerian Professor of Chemistry.

moments.name: Faraday Discovers Electromagnetic Induction at the Royal Institution
moments.subtitle: A self-taught scientist with no math beyond algebra invents the principle behind every power station on Earth
moments.description: On 29 August 1831, Michael Faraday demonstrated electromagnetic induction at the Royal Institution in London, showing that a changing magnetic field could produce an electric current in a wire. The discovery, which Faraday described using his concept of 'lines of force,' provided the operating principle for the electrical transformer and generator. James Clerk Maxwell would later translate Faraday's visual intuitions into the mathematical equations that underpin all modern electromagnetic theory. Faraday's discovery made the large-scale generation and distribution of electricity possible, transforming civilization.

moments.name: Faraday Turns Down a Knighthood, Saying He Prefers to Remain 'Plain Mr Faraday'
moments.subtitle: The most celebrated scientist in Victorian Britain rejects worldly honors on religious grounds
moments.description: During the 1830s and 1840s, Michael Faraday was offered a knighthood and twice refused the presidency of the Royal Society. A devout member of the Sandemanian church, Faraday believed that accumulating riches and pursuing worldly reward was against Biblical teaching. He told colleagues he preferred to remain 'plain Mr Faraday to the end.' In 1832, Oxford granted him an honorary doctorate, and he was elected to scientific academies across Europe, but Faraday consistently rejected titles of personal aggrandizement. Einstein later kept Faraday's portrait on his study wall alongside Newton and Maxwell.

moments.name: Faraday Dies at Hampton Court After Declining Burial at Westminster Abbey
moments.subtitle: A scientist who refused every honor in life also refused the grandest honor in death
moments.description: On 25 August 1867, Michael Faraday died at his grace-and-favour house at Hampton Court, aged 75. The house had been granted to him by Queen Victoria's consort Prince Albert in 1848. Faraday had years earlier turned down an offer of burial in Westminster Abbey, consistent with his lifelong rejection of worldly honors. He was instead buried in the dissenters' section of Highgate Cemetery. A memorial plaque was later placed in Westminster Abbey near Isaac Newton's tomb. Faraday's discoveries in electromagnetism and electrochemistry had made the modern electrical age possible, yet he died as he lived: deliberately humble.
moments.address: 37 Hampton Court Road, Hampton Court, London
